method: Constructed author examples of minimally adequate complete performances; hand-scored against the essential criteria, not learner observations or an automated semantic grader.

examples.exampleEn: A: The horizontal scale measures elapsed hours and the vertical scale litres. At 3 h the straight segment gives A halfway between 50 and 60, hence 55 L; B is 50 L. B: Bus/Material name expense items rather than numerical values; the horizontal numbers count hundreds of euro. Bus is 2.5 hundreds, 250 EUR; Material is 4 hundreds, 400 EUR, so Material is greater. No prescribed term category, no separate subtraction and no repeated prose multiplier are required.

A is highest at 60 L after 4 h; A and B have the same 50 L after 2 and 6 h. A gains 10 L in each first 2-hour interval, then loses 10 L in the last 2 hours; B stays constant. A is below B until 2 h and above between the equalities in the shown period. C stays at its maximum 50 L from 1 to 3 h; it gains 30 L in the first hour, remains constant for 2 hours and then loses 20 L in 2 hours. Nothing in the graph fixes later behavior; a volume decrease alone does not identify a pump. Quotient notation and formal closed-interval notation are unnecessary.

A cannot be triple: 3 times 40 would be 120 L, whereas B is 60 L. The drawn heights above 30 L are 10 and 30, so it is those differences whose ratio is 3, not the entire volumes; that is why this full-volume-ratio inference fails, rather than every crop being forbidden. In B both increases are 10 L, but one takes 1 h and one 4 h, so the second rate is one quarter of the first. Equal drawing widths hide this unequal time base, making equal drawn slopes misleading for rates. Decimal division is unnecessary.

A: the visible heights above 30 L compare 10 with 30, but the full volumes are 40 and 60, so the quantity is not triple. I would use a table headed Container | Volume in L | Ratio to A, with A | 40 | 1 and B | 60 | 1.5. It makes the full-volume base explicit instead of comparing differences above 30. B: 27 exceeds 24 as a count, but 24/40 is 60% and 27/60 is 45%, so A has the greater share. I would use a table Group | Participants | Total | Proportion, A | 24 | 40 | 60%, B | 27 | 60 | 45%. The proportion column puts different group sizes on the same whole-group base, while the counts and totals remain visible. No chart is mandatory.
